n: Hezekiah becomes king of Judah. His reign is one of the brightest in Judah’s history, and chapters 18–20 are nearly identical to Isaiah 36–39.
He took the throne at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years (about 715–686 BC, with an earlier co-regency).
He is the first king since David to be praised without reservation: he did right just as David did.

f.w: according to all that David his father did

n: He removed the high places, smashed sacred pillars, cut down Asherah poles, and even destroyed the bronze serpent Moses had made, because people were burning incense to it. He called it “Nehushtan”—just a piece of bronze. A sacred symbol of Christ had been turned into an idol.

f.w: the brasen serpent that Moses had made

f.g: a wordplay on nehoshet (bronze) and nahash (serpent): ‘a bronze thing.’

n: Hezekiah’s defining quality is trust in the Lord. No king of Judah, before or after, matched him in this.
He held fast to the Lord, never turning away, and kept the commandments given through Moses.
The Lord was with him, and he succeeded. He boldly rebelled against Assyria, refusing to remain a vassal as his father Ahaz had chosen to be.
He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza, everywhere from small outposts to walled cities.

f.w: from the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city
f.g: everywhere, from small to large settlements.

n: The narrator recalls the siege of Samaria, which began in Hezekiah’s fourth year—a sober backdrop to his reign.
Samaria fell after three years, in 722 BC.
Israel was deported to distant lands in Assyria and Media.
The reason is restated: Israel broke the covenant and would not listen. Judah now faces the same empire—will it trust the Lord?

In 701 BC, Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah and captures its fortified cities. His own records boast of taking forty-six walled towns and shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage.”
Hezekiah sends word to Sennacherib at Lachish, admitting fault and offering to pay whatever is required. Assyria demands about 11 tons of silver and one ton of gold.

f.g: Judah’s second city; Assyrian palace reliefs depict its capture.

n: Hezekiah empties the treasuries of temple and palace.
He even strips the gold he himself had put on the temple doors and doorposts. In fear, his first response is to pay, not to pray.
Despite the payment, Sennacherib sends three high officials with a large army to demand Jerusalem’s surrender. They stand at the very spot where Isaiah had once confronted Ahaz.

f.g: a title: chief cupbearer, a high official and spokesman.

f.w: the conduit of the upper pool

n: Three of Hezekiah’s officials come out to negotiate: Eliakim, the palace administrator; Shebna, the secretary; and Joah, the recorder.
The Rabshakeh’s speech is a masterpiece of psychological warfare. His central question: “What are you trusting in?”
He mocks Judah’s military strategy and alliances as empty words.
Egypt, he says, is a cracked reed—lean on it and it will pierce your hand. On this point, Isaiah actually agreed.

f.w: the staff of this bruised reed

n: Cleverly, he claims Hezekiah offended the Lord by removing His altars—twisting Hezekiah’s reforms into sacrilege, as if the many shrines had honored God.
He taunts them: “I’ll give you two thousand horses—if you can even find riders for them.”

f.g: make a wager, strike a bargain.

n: How could Judah resist even the lowest Assyrian officer?
His boldest claim: the Lord Himself sent Assyria to destroy Judah. There was a grain of truth—Isaiah called Assyria the rod of God’s anger—but Assyria’s arrogance would also be judged.
Hezekiah’s officials ask him to speak Aramaic, the diplomatic language, rather than Hebrew, so the people on the wall won’t understand.

f.g: Aramaic, the international diplomatic language of the time.

n: The Rabshakeh refuses—his message is aimed at the common people, who will face starvation in a siege. His crude language describes the horrors of famine.
He shouts in Hebrew directly to the people on the wall.
“Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you—he can’t save you.”
“Don’t let him persuade you to trust the Lord.” The real battle is over faith.
He offers a peaceful surrender: each person will enjoy his own vine, fig tree, and cistern—images of security that scripture uses for the messianic age.

f.w: eat ye every man of his own vine

n: Until, he admits, Assyria deports them to a land “like your own.” It is Satan’s pattern: a counterfeit promised land in exchange for surrendering one’s covenant identity.

f.w: a land like your own land

n: He points out that no nation’s god has stopped Assyria.
He lists conquered cities whose gods failed—including Samaria. To him, the Lord is just another local god.
“Which god has saved his country from me? Why would the LORD save Jerusalem?” This blasphemy sets up the Lord’s answer in chapter 19.

f.w: that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem

n: The people stay silent, as Hezekiah had ordered. Sometimes the wisest response to mockery is silence.
The three officials return to Hezekiah with torn clothes, a sign of grief and alarm, and report everything.
